docs.title: orm-loader
docs.text:
A lightweight, reusable foundation for building and validating SQLAlchemy-based data models.

orm-loader provides infrastructure for SQLAlchemy-based data models. It is the shared plumbing layer, not the place where model-specific rules live.

It focuses on:

  • ORM table introspection
  • safe bulk ingestion patterns
  • file-based loading via staging tables
  • model-agnostic validation scaffolding
  • operational helpers for supported backends

It ships with backend implementations for SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB. See oa-configurator's supported dialects for the dialect list this is built against.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Tables are structural — semantics live downstream
  • Mixins define capabilities
  • Protocols decouple infrastructure from implementations
  • Ingestion is explicit and staged

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• Tables
  • Registry & Validation
  • Loaders

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
orm-loader is intentionally conservative. It gives downstream libraries the machinery to load, inspect, and validate data without deciding what the data means.

The library is designed to sit below:

  • OMOP CDM (initial scope)
  • extension to O3, MCODE, etc.
  • custom clinical schemas
  • research data marts

and above:

  • raw SQLAlchemy
  • database-specific ingestion scripts

docs.title: What this library does not do
docs.text:
• No domain validation
  • No schema enforcement
  • No migrations
  • No concurrency guarantees
  • No support yet for arbitrary database dialects

docs.title: Why mixins and protocols?
docs.text:
Mixins provide reusable behaviour.

Protocols provide: - static typing - runtime structural checks - decoupling between infrastructure and models

This allows downstream libraries to: - replace base classes - mock implementations - incrementally adopt features

docs.title: Loaders
docs.text:
orm_loader.loaders loads files into staging tables. A file takes the same path on every backend and in every format:

flowchart LR A[File] --> B[FileReader] B --> C[Arrow record batches] C --> D[BatchProcessor with the ConversionPolicy] D --> E[Backend sink] E --> F[Staging table]

Loading is infrastructure only. It carries no domain rules, streams files in bounded batches, and fails visibly instead of changing data.

Page Covers Readers FileReader, the provided readers, format detection and how to add a format Conversion The policy that turns raw values into column types, and the column handlers Staging and sinks stage_file, the backend sinks, deduplication and normalise Context and report LoaderContext, LoadReport and row accounting

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. A reader is chosen from the file suffix, or passed explicitly, and yields the file as batches.
  2. Each batch is converted to the ORM column types under the conversion policy. With normalise=False values are written as read.
  3. The backend's bulk sink writes the batch into the staging table.
  4. The staging table is optionally deduplicated.
  5. The number of rows left in staging is returned, and the table layer merges them into the target.

Staging tables isolate a load from the production table, which makes rollback safe and merges repeatable. Merge behaviour belongs to the table mixins and the backend layer, not to the loader.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• Ingestion is deterministic and no value is silently changed or lost.
  • Every row read is loaded, rejected to a rejects file, or dropped as a duplicate. A load that cannot account for every row raises.
  • Domain rules stay outside the loader.

The loader does not guarantee the correctness of the source data.

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text:
orm_loader.conversion interprets raw values for every file load, whatever the file format.

flowchart LR A[Arrow column] --> B[Policy picks the column's handler] B --> C[clean] C --> D[detect missing] D --> E[parse] E --> F[check] F --> G[values and invalid mask]

docs.title: ConversionPolicy
docs.text:
ConversionPolicy is a frozen settings object passed to load_file(policy=...). It holds the settings shared by every column and one handler for each kind of column type.

Field Meaning nulls NullPolicy: what counts as a missing value errors ErrorPolicy: what happens to unreadable and missing required values text, integer, floating, numeric, boolean, date, datetime The handler for that kind of column, each with its own settings handlers Handlers for further column types, or replacements, by SQLAlchemy type class columns Handlers for single columns by (table_name, column_name) 
policy = ConversionPolicy(
    nulls=NullPolicy(text_markers=frozenset({"NULL"})),
    errors=ErrorPolicy(on_error="reject_row", max_rejects=0.01),
    date=DateHandler(formats=("dd/mm/yyyy",)),
    columns={("concept", "concept_code"): TextHandler(strip=False)},
)

The settings of one load, shared by every column.

The handler for a column is, in order, the entry in columns and the handler for the most specific class of the column type (the stored type of a TypeDecorator) among handlers and the built-in fields. A column type with no handler is an error.

docs.title: NullPolicy
docs.text:
• Text columns keep every nonempty value verbatim. Only empty and whitespace-only text is null.
  • Words such as NULL, None, N/A and NaN stay as text in text columns. Version 2 turned them into NULL, which dropped concepts with those names. To treat words as missing again, list them in text_markers, for example NullPolicy(text_markers=frozenset({"NULL", "None", "N/A", "NaN", "nan", "null", "NA", "n/a"})). Set operations add or remove words from a set you keep.
  • text_markers are exact, case-sensitive words that are null in every text column of the load. Matching ignores surrounding whitespace and applies the same way to every file format. To treat a word as missing in some columns only, subclass TextHandler, override missing() and register it in ConversionPolicy.columns.
  • empty_is_null=False keeps empty text fields as empty strings. Typed columns still treat empty fields as missing.
  • Typed columns accept a valid value, a missing word (null, none, na, n/a, nan and similar) or a real null, and fail otherwise.

What counts as a missing value, shared by every column handler.

Text columns keep every nonempty value verbatim apart from the markers. Typed columns treat empty text and the typed missing words as missing.

Attributes:

Name Type Description empty_is_null bool

Empty and whitespace-only text becomes null in text columns.

text_markers frozenset[str]

Exact, case-sensitive text values treated as missing in text columns. Matching ignores surrounding whitespace.

docs.title: ErrorPolicy
docs.text:
on_error is raise (default) or reject_row. max_rejects stops a reject_row load before the merge. A count stops the load as soon as it is passed, and a fraction is checked once all rows have been read, against the total number of rows read. A load that rejected rows logs a warning with their number and the rejects file.

What happens to a row with an unreadable value or a missing required value.

Attributes:

Name Type Description on_error Literal['raise', 'reject_row']

"raise" aborts on the first batch containing such a row. "reject_row" drops those rows and writes them to a rejects file.

max_rejects float | None

With reject_row, abort once rejected rows exceed this count, or this fraction of rows read when it is a float between 0 and 1.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
The handler for a column is the first match of: the entry in ConversionPolicy.columns and the handler for the most specific class of the column type. A TypeDecorator is handled as the type it stores. A column type with no handler is an error that names the table, column and type, raised before any row is processed. Loading such a column unchanged is an explicit choice: columns={("table", "column"): PassthroughHandler()}.

Handler Column types Accepted text Settings TextHandler String, Text Any nonempty text; longer than the column is an error strip EnumHandler Enum One of the labels the column stores strip IntegerHandler Integer, SmallInteger, BigInteger Optional sign and digits, with an optional all-zero fraction (1.0); a value outside the 16, 32 or 64 bits of the column type is an error none FloatHandler Float Decimal or exponent form; Infinity and values that overflow to infinity are errors none NumericHandler Numeric Plain and exponent decimal forms such as 1.5, .05 and 1.5E3, converted to an Arrow decimal of the declared precision and scale without rounding; a precision without a scale has scale 0. A value that does not fit the declared digits is an error. The declaration must have a precision of at most 38 digits, see below none BooleanHandler Boolean true, t, yes, y, 1, on and their opposites true_words, false_words DateHandler Date One of formats, validated against the calendar; year 0 is an error formats DateTimeHandler DateTime ISO date and time, or a date in one of formats; see time zones below formats

Dates default to yyyymmdd, dd-mon-yyyy and yyyy-mm-dd. Ambiguous forms such as 02/01/2020 are never guessed; declare DateHandler(formats=("dd/mm/yyyy",)) or ("mm/dd/yyyy",). A timestamp column reads date-only values with its own formats.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The column type decides, so no value is converted by a convention the schema did not ask for.

  • A DateTime(timezone=True) column requires an offset (Z or +hh:mm) and stores UTC. A value without an offset and a date-only value are errors.
  • A DateTime column without a time zone rejects a value with an offset.

docs.title: Typed input
docs.text:
Input that already has a type, such as a Parquet column, is cast to the column type and checked like parsed text. A value that does not come back unchanged when cast back to its input type is an error, so an integer 2 in a Boolean column, a timestamp with a time in a Date column and a decimal that loses digits are all rejected. Float NaN is missing.

In a Numeric column an integer is read exactly and a float is read as its shortest decimal text, so a Parquet float column loads the same values as a CSV of the same numbers. Infinity is an error.

docs.title: Numeric columns
docs.text: The loader converts only what an Arrow decimal can hold, which is a precision of at most 38 digits. That is also the widest decimal DuckDB stores, and SQLite stores Numeric as a float. A Numeric column with a wider precision or no precision raises a PolicyError before any row is read. To load it anyway, leave the value to the database with columns={("table", "column"): PassthroughHandler()}: the database then parses the text and rounds a value that exceeds the scale, and a value it cannot parse aborts the load.

docs.title: Adding a column type
docs.text:
Subclass ConvertingHandler, implement arrow_type and parse, and pass the handler in ConversionPolicy.handlers for the type class, or in ConversionPolicy.columns for a single column. clean, missing and check can be overridden.

class HexHandler(ConvertingHandler):
    def arrow_type(self, sa_type):
        return pa.int64()

    def parse(self, cleaned, sa_type):
        ...  # return Interpretation(values, invalid)

policy = ConversionPolicy(handlers={MyHexType: HexHandler()})

docs.title: ConvertingHandler
docs.text:
Bases: ColumnHandler

Converts a column in four stages: clean, detect missing, parse, check.

Text input follows the stages. Input that already has a type, such as a Parquet column, is cast directly with floating NaN read as missing. A value that does not survive the cast back to its input type is lossy and unreadable, and check runs on the cast values. Subclasses supply arrow_type and parse and may override clean, missing and check.

Attributes:

Name Type Description distinct bool

Run the stages once per distinct value and gather the results back, for types whose parse step is expensive per value.

docs.title: Readers
docs.text:
A reader yields a file as Arrow record batches holding the model columns present in the file. Text formats yield raw strings, so the conversion policy sees exactly what the file contains. Typed formats yield their stored types. A reader decides nothing about missing values: an empty field is an empty string, and the null policy is applied afterwards.

open_reader picks the reader from the file suffix: .parquet is read as Parquet, any other suffix as delimited text. load_file opens the reader with it, taking quote_mode and chunksize as arguments, and load_file(reader=...) passes a configured reader explicitly.

Reader Input DelimitedTextReader Delimited text with a tab or comma delimiter and detected encoding ParquetReader Parquet files, in batches of chunksize rows

docs.title: Staging and Sinks
docs.text:
stage_file(ctx, reader, staging) connects a reader, the batch processor and the sink of the session's backend. It loads into the given staging table, respects the LoaderContext flags, returns the number of rows left in staging, and leaves the merge to the table layer.

Load a file into the staging table.

The reader streams the file in bounded batches, so memory does not grow with the row count. A file without data rows loads nothing and is not checked for required columns. With ctx.dedupe set, the staging table keeps the first row for each primary key. A failure after the first write rolls the session back; DuckDB commits every few batches, so earlier batches stay committed there.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ctx LoaderContext

Loader context.

required reader FileReader

Reader that yields the file as Arrow batches.

required staging Table

Staging table the rows are written to.

required

Returns:

Type Description int

Number of rows left in the staging table.

Raises:

Type Description IngestError

The file cannot be read, is missing a required column, or the rows read are not all accounted for.

ConversionError

A value cannot be read as its column type.

RequiredValueError

A required column has no value.

RejectLimitError

Rejected rows exceed ErrorPolicy.max_rejects.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Values are interpreted by column type, as described in Conversion.
  • With the default policy an unreadable value or a missing required value raises and nothing is loaded.
  • With ErrorPolicy(on_error="reject_row") those rows, and delimited lines with the wrong number of fields, are written to <rejects_dir>/<file name>.rejects.csv and the rest load. A malformed line is listed with its row number in the file, and its text is in the reason. rejects_dir defaults to a rejects directory inside the input file's directory, and the file of an earlier load is removed. LoadReport accounts for every row read, checked against the rows counted in the staging table.
  • With normalise=False raw text is passed to the staging table unchanged, empty fields included, without literal defaults, non-key required checks or type conversion. SQL-expression defaults still apply to null staging values during merge. Primary-key columns must still be present. What the database does with a value that does not fit its column then depends on the dialect.
  • A blank value, and a column the file lacks, take the column's default when it has one: a server default written as text, a scalar Python default, or a SQL expression such as current_date. Literal defaults are converted by the column's handler. SQL expressions are applied in the merge with COALESCE, so the database evaluates them once for each row that needs a default. A column with a callable default stays required.

docs.title: Staging table
docs.text: Staging mirrors the target’s loadable columns and types, excluding computed columns, with no key, index, default or constraint, and a _rownum column that orders the rows (SQLite uses its rowid). Columns with SQL-expression defaults allow NULL in staging so the merge can apply their defaults. Other columns preserve the target’s nullability. Every column that is required and has no default must be in the file, primary key columns included, so a file without its key fails before anything is loaded.

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
Each backend uses the fastest bulk interface its engine offers.

Backend Sink PostgreSQL One COPY from Arrow-written CSV DuckDB Insert from a temporary view over the Arrow batch, committed every five batches SQLite Native executemany per batch

A failure in the sink is raised. There is no fallback to another loading path.

docs.title: Deduplication
docs.text: With dedupe set, the staging table keeps the first row for each primary key, in source order. The backend removes the others after the load and reports a DedupeResult on LoadReport with the rows before and the rows removed. The merge step decides what happens when incoming rows overlap with existing target rows.

docs.title: Merge strategies
docs.text:
Each strategy does what its name says, whatever the target already holds.

Strategy Effect replace Deletes target rows whose primary key is in the file, then inserts the file upsert Inserts the file and skips rows whose primary key already exists, keeping the first of a repeated key insert Inserts the file without any key check, so a key that already exists fails with the database's duplicate key error

insert suits a first load into an empty table, or any file whose keys are new. With dedupe=True it is several times faster than upsert, because upsert checks every row against the key index. A load with upsert into an empty table logs this hint and runs unchanged.

With merge_batch_size set, PostgreSQL and DuckDB commit the session after each merge batch. If a later batch or deferred-key validation fails, earlier target batches stay committed, along with any other pending session work. A replace failure can leave some rows deleted or updated. SQLite keeps the batches in the caller's transaction. Use batching only when you can accept partial results and the session has no unrelated pending work.

No schema changes are performed at the loader layer.

docs.title: Referential integrity
docs.text:
On PostgreSQL and SQLite a load relaxes foreign keys from before it writes staging until it has merged, so the caller needs no foreign key handling and a row loaded before the row it references is accepted. SQLite ignores PRAGMA foreign_keys inside a transaction, so a session with uncommitted writes cannot start a load there and load_file raises before touching anything. To verify the result, call Table.validate_foreign_keys(session) after every table is loaded. It checks every foreign key of the table with an anti-join and raises ForeignKeyViolationError with up to five unmatched keys. Null references are not violations, and the load order does not matter.

To insert ORM objects built in Python that reference each other, wrap the inserts in backend.relaxed_foreign_keys(session), which relaxes the keys on PostgreSQL and SQLite and leaves them enforced on DuckDB.

Autoflush is suspended by default. Flush the pending inserts inside the block so they run while checks are relaxed:

with backend.relaxed_foreign_keys(session):
    session.add_all(objects)
    session.flush()
session.commit()

On PostgreSQL, relaxation is transaction-local and is reapplied when a new transaction begins, even if the session switches pooled connections. Exiting the scope restores the prior role on any transaction still active.

DuckDB enforces the keys it creates, so load parent tables first. load_file already validates the keys DuckDB never enforces (cross-schema, cyclic and self-referential) after each table's merge, and validate_foreign_keys repeats that check, so it works the same way on every backend. A DuckDB table with foreign keys needs resolved= for both.

docs.title: Model Registry & Validation
docs.text:
The orm_loader.registry module provides model-agnostic validation infrastructure for SQLAlchemy ORM models.

It enables: - loading external table / field specifications - registering ORM models - structural comparison between models and specs - reusable validation rules - structured validation reports

This layer is schema-aware but domain-agnostic.

docs.title: End-to-End Validation Example
docs.text:
This example demonstrates the complete validation workflow:

  1. Load external specifications
  2. Register ORM models
  3. Run validation
  4. Inspect and consume validation results

docs.title: External specifications
docs.text:
Validation begins with external table and field specifications (e.g. OMOP CSVs):

  • tables.csv — table-level definitions
  • fields.csv — field-level definitions

These describe what should exist, not how it is implemented.

docs.title: ORM models
docs.text:
Assume you have SQLAlchemy ORM models defined elsewhere:

from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base
from orm_loader.tables import ORMTableBase

Base = declarative_base()

class Person(ORMTableBase, Base):
    __tablename__ = "person"
    # columns omitted for brevity

class VisitOccurrence(ORMTableBase, Base):
    __tablename__ = "visit_occurrence"
    # columns omitted for brevity

docs.title: 2. Create a ModelRegistry
docs.text:
The registry is the coordination object that holds models and specs.

from orm_loader.registry import ModelRegistry

registry = ModelRegistry(
    model_version="5.4",
    model_name="OMOP"
)

docs.title: 3. Load Specifications
docs.text:
Specifications are loaded from CSV resources:

from importlib.resources import files

specs = files("my_specs_package")

registry.load_table_specs(
    table_csv=specs / "tables.csv",
    field_csv=specs / "fields.csv",
)
At this point, the registry knows:

  • which tables are required
  • which fields belong to each table
  • primary and foreign key expectations

docs.title: 4. Register ORM models
docs.text:
Models can be registered explicitly:

registry.register_models([
    Person,
    VisitOccurrence,
])

Or discovered automatically from a package:

registry.discover_models("my_project.models")

Each model is introspected into a ModelDescriptor.

docs.title: 5. Inspect Registry State
docs.text:
Before running validation, the registry can be queried:

registry.known_tables()
registry.registered_tables()
registry.missing_required_tables()
This supports pre-flight checks and early failure in CI pipelines.

docs.title: 6. Define Validators
docs.text:
Validators are small, composable rule objects:

from orm_loader.registry.validation import (
    ColumnPresenceValidator,
    ColumnNullabilityValidator,
    PrimaryKeyValidator,
    ForeignKeyShapeValidator,
)

validators = [
    ColumnPresenceValidator(),
    ColumnNullabilityValidator(),
    PrimaryKeyValidator(),
    ForeignKeyShapeValidator(),
]

Each validator:

  • operates on a single model
  • produces structured validation issues
  • is independent of execution order

docs.title: 7. Run Validation
docs.text:
Validation is coordinated by the ValidationRunner:

from orm_loader.registry.validation_runner import ValidationRunner

runner = ValidationRunner(
    validators=validators,
    fail_fast=False,
)

report = runner.run(registry)

docs.title: Overall Validity
docs.text: report.is_valid()

docs.title: Top Level Summary
docs.text: print(report.summary())

docs.title: Human-readable report
docs.text: print(report.render_text_report())

docs.title: Machine-readable output (CI/CD)
docs.text: report.to_dict()

docs.title: ModelRegistry
docs.text:
The ModelRegistry is the central coordination object for model registration and validation.

It holds: - registered ORM models - external table specifications - external field specifications - derived model descriptors

The registry does not perform validation itself — it provides the context required for validators and runners.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Load table and field specifications
  • Register ORM model classes
  • Track required vs implemented tables
  • Provide descriptors for validation

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Holds a registry of ORM models along with their specifications.

The registry coordinates: - loading table and field specifications - registering ORM model classes - identifying missing or required tables - providing model descriptors for validation

Load table and field specifications from CSV files (currently only OMOP format supported). TODO: support generalised specification formats via LinkML or similar.

Register ORM model classes and compare against specifications to confirm accurate and complete implementation.

Model-specific constraints can be created to extend context-specific validation such as OMOP domain constraints, value set adherence, etc.

Validation logic itself is implemented elsewhere and consumes the registry as contextual input.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Simple in-process ID allocator.

This utility provides monotonically increasing integer identifiers starting from a known baseline. It is intended for environments where database-managed sequences are unavailable or undesirable.

Typical use cases include: - SQLite or other lightweight databases without sequences - controlled, single-writer ingestion pipelines - deterministic ID assignment during bulk loads

This allocator is deliberately minimal and not safe for concurrent writers or multi-process use.

docs.title: Loadable Table Mixins
docs.text:
Infrastructure for staged, file-based ingestion into ORM tables.

Supports: - staged file loading into backend-specific staging tables - bulk staging sinks per backend: PostgreSQL COPY, DuckDB insert from Arrow, SQLite executemany - backend-aware merge strategies - Arrow-based file readers (delimited text and Parquet) - index handling during merge

docs.title: FileLoadableTableInterface
docs.text:
Bases: ORMTableBase

Mixin for ORM tables that load from files through a staging table.

A file is read in batches by a reader, converted under a conversion policy, written to a staging table by the backend's bulk sink, and merged into the target table. It supports: - dialect-aware staging table creation - delimited text and Parquet files, and other formats through readers - configurable merge strategies - explicit staging table lifecycle management

The class is designed for controlled ingestion pipelines and does not attempt to provide concurrency guarantees.

docs.title: load_file(session, path, *, reader=None, normalise=True, dedupe=False, chunksize=None, merge_strategy='replace', quote_mode=None, index_strategy='auto', merge_batch_size=None, staging_schema_tag=None, validate_deferred_fks=True, resolved=None, physical_schemas=None, policy=None, rejects_dir=None, report=None) classmethod
docs.text:
Load a file into the target table.

The file name without its suffix must equal the table name. This method orchestrates the full staged ingestion lifecycle: - staging table creation - file loading - merge into the target table - staging table cleanup

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default session Session

An active SQLAlchemy session.

required path Path

Path to the input file.

required reader FileReader | None

Reader for the file. open_reader chooses one from the file suffix when omitted, and chunksize and quote_mode then configure it. Passing either together with a reader is an error, because the reader is already configured.

None normalise bool

Whether to convert values to the column types under the policy. When false, values are written as read.

True dedupe bool

Whether to deduplicate incoming rows.

False chunksize int | None

Rows per batch for the default reader of formats that batch by rows.

None merge_strategy str

Merge strategy to apply (e.g. replace, upsert, or insert).

'replace' quote_mode str | None

How double quotes in delimited text are read: "csv" (field quoting), "literal" (kept as data), "by_delimiter" (literal for tab-delimited files, field quoting otherwise).

None index_strategy str

Index handling strategy during merge. Use "auto" to let the backend choose a sensible default.

'auto' merge_batch_size int | None

Rows per merge batch, or None to merge in one statement. On PostgreSQL and DuckDB, each merge batch commits the session. A later failure leaves earlier target batches committed, along with any other pending session work. SQLite keeps the batches in the caller's transaction.

None staging_schema_tag str | None

schema_translate_map tag the staging table lives in. None means no schema qualification (backend-default behavior). Threaded through every internal step of the load lifecycle so they all resolve the same backend/schema.

None validate_deferred_fks bool

After merging, run an anti-join check for any FK this backend's DB can't enforce itself (see DatabaseBackend.validate_deferred_fks()). Also run before every intermediate commit a batched merge makes, so a violation is caught before that batch commits rather than only after the whole load, when an earlier batch's commit can no longer be rolled back. Every other key is verified by validate_foreign_keys.

True resolved ResolvedDatabase | None

Topology this table's engine(s) were resolved from. Required on DuckDB whenever table_cls has any foreign key at all, to classify each as enforced or omitted via oa-configurator's unenforced_foreign_keys(); omitting it raises rather than guessing. Ignored by every other backend, and by a DuckDB table with no foreign keys.

None physical_schemas Mapping[str, str | None] | None

A schema tag's physical name beyond resolved's own configured ones. Forwarded alongside resolved.

None policy ConversionPolicy | None

How values are interpreted and what happens to unreadable ones. The default policy preserves nonempty text and treats only empty values as missing in text columns.

None rejects_dir Path | None

Directory that rejected rows are written to when the policy sets on_error="reject_row", as <file name>.rejects.csv. Defaults to a rejects directory inside the source file's directory.

None report LoadReport | None

Receives the load's row accounting. A new report is used when omitted.

None

Returns:

Type Description int

Number of rows loaded into staging before merge.

docs.title: validate_foreign_keys(session, *, staging_schema_tag=None, resolved=None, physical_schemas=None) classmethod
docs.text:
Raise if any row references a row that does not exist.

Loads relax foreign keys during the merge on PostgreSQL and SQLite, so a row loaded before the row it references is accepted. Call this once every table is loaded to verify referential integrity, whatever the load order. DuckDB enforces most of its keys itself, so only the keys it cannot enforce are checked.

None

docs.title: Materialized Views
docs.text:
Materialized views are database-maintained read models: a stored Select whose result can be queried like a table and rebuilt when its source data changes. They are useful when a downstream application repeatedly performs the same expensive join, filter, or aggregation.

This page describes the contract that downstream packages should depend on. The implementation lives in orm_loader; consumers should declare a view once and call its lifecycle methods rather than reproducing the DDL themselves.

docs.title: The ownership boundary
docs.text:
orm_loader owns the physical materialized-view lifecycle:

  1. create the view from __mv_select__;
  2. create its declared indexes;
  3. refresh views in dependency order; and
  4. drop views during teardown or replacement.

The consumer owns when those operations happen. A typical application creates views during database setup, loads or updates its source tables, and refreshes the views as part of the same operational workflow. A view is not a second source of truth: its Select and declarations in code are the source of truth, while the database object is a refreshable read cache.

This is deliberately separate from the ordinary ORM table mixins and from the loader lifecycle. Loaders populate source tables; materialized-view orchestration makes derived read models available after that work has completed.

docs.title: Declare the read model once
docs.text:
The class declaration is the integration point that downstream code can import and reuse. It names the physical view, defines its contents, records materialized-view dependencies, and optionally declares indexes.

class RecentObservationMV(Base, MaterializedViewMixin):
    __mv_name__ = "mv_recent_observation"
    __mv_select__ = (
        sa.select(
            Observation.observation_id,
            Observation.person_id,
            Observation.observation_date,
            Observation.value_as_number,
        )
        .where(
            Observation.observation_date
            >= sa.func.current_date() - sa.text("INTERVAL '30 days'")
        )
    )
    __mv_dependencies__ = {"observation"}
    __mv_indexes__ = (
        MaterializedViewIndex(
            name="mv_recent_observation_id_uq",
            columns=("observation_id",),
            unique=True,
        ),
    )

The mixin can also be used without an ORM mapping when the view is consumed through SQLAlchemy Core. When it is combined with a declarative base, the class can additionally describe how application code queries the resulting rows. In both cases, keep the physical name and lifecycle declaration in one shared class so setup code and query code cannot drift apart.

__mv_dependencies__ may contain source-table names as documentation. Only names that belong to the list passed to resolve_mv_refresh_order participate in the topological sort. This means a source table does not need to be registered as a materialized view, while dependencies between registered materialized views are refreshed in the correct order.

docs.title: A safe lifecycle
docs.text:
For a collection of views, make the refresh list explicit and share it between setup and refresh jobs:

ALL_MVS = [RecentObservationMV, DailyObservationCountsMV]

for view in ALL_MVS:
    view.create_mv(engine)

# Run after the source-table load or update has committed.
refresh_all_mvs(engine, ALL_MVS)

create_mv() is idempotent with its default if_not_exists=True, but it does not compare or migrate an existing definition. If __mv_select__ changes, the consumer must choose a replacement/migration strategy; calling create_mv() again will not rewrite the existing view.

refresh_all_mvs() is the useful boundary for downstream orchestration. It sorts the supplied classes and raises RuntimeError for a dependency cycle. Refreshing one class directly is appropriate when the caller already knows that its prerequisites are current.

docs.title: Choose creation and refresh semantics deliberately
docs.text:
Operation Default Consumer decision create_mv() Create and populate the view; create declared indexes Use with_data=False when population should happen in a later refresh; use create_indexes=False only when index creation is managed elsewhere refresh_mv() Blocking refresh Use concurrently=True only when the declaration includes a simple unique index that is created in the target database drop_mv() IF EXISTS, no cascade Use cascade=True only when dependent database objects should be removed as part of teardown

with_data=False leaves a newly created view uninitialized. It must be refreshed before consumers query it. if_not_exists=False and drop_mv(if_exists=False) are useful when setup should fail loudly instead of treating an existing or missing object as acceptable.

The lower-level DDL contracts are available for migration systems that need to compose statements themselves, but most downstream code should use the mixin methods so indexes and refresh eligibility remain tied to the declaration.

docs.title: Concurrent refresh is a declaration-and-database contract
docs.text:
PostgreSQL permits REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY only when the view has a suitable simple unique index. Declare that index with MaterializedViewIndex(unique=True) in __mv_indexes__:

class PatientSummaryMV(MaterializedViewMixin):
    __mv_name__ = "mv_patient_summary"
    __mv_select__ = patient_summary_select
    __mv_indexes__ = (
        MaterializedViewIndex(
            name="mv_patient_summary_patient_id_uq",
            columns=("patient_id",),
            unique=True,
        ),
    )


PatientSummaryMV.create_mv(engine)
PatientSummaryMV.refresh_mv(engine, concurrently=True)

create_mv() creates declared indexes immediately after the view. The concurrently=True pre-check is intentionally cheap and conservative: it checks the declaration before issuing SQL, then lets PostgreSQL verify that the index really exists and is valid. If no unique index is declared, or if PostgreSQL rejects the concurrent refresh, the operation raises ConcurrentRefreshNotEligibleError without hiding the underlying cause.

This is fail-closed by design. An index created manually outside __mv_indexes__ does not satisfy the mixin's declaration contract; declare it in the class even if another migration is responsible for creating it. Expressions, partial indexes, and other index forms are outside this simple contract and should not be represented as MaterializedViewIndex entries.

The view's physical schema comes from the bound connection's own schema_translate_map. create_mv()/refresh_mv()/drop_mv() resolve it via oa_configurator.physical_schema_of() before ever reaching the backend, which only ever sees an already-resolved physical schema string.

The schema tag itself comes from one of three places, in order:

  1. an explicit schema_tag= argument, for a one-off override;
  2. when the class is also declaratively mapped (combined with a Base, with a real __table__), that table's own schema -- set the schema the same way as any other mapped table, via __table_args__ = {"schema": ...}, and the materialized view follows it automatically;
  3. __mv_schema_tag__ (defaults to "primary"), only consulted for a Core-only declaration with no mapped table to derive anything from.
# Core-only: no Base, no mapped table, so __mv_schema_tag__ is what resolves it.
class VocabSummaryMV(MaterializedViewMixin):
    __mv_name__ = "vocab_summary"
    __mv_select__ = ...
    __mv_schema_tag__ = Role.VOCAB.value  # resolves via the connection's vocab schema

# Uses __mv_schema_tag__ ("primary" by default) via the connection's own schema_translate_map.
RecentObservationMV.create_mv(engine)

# Override for one call.
RecentObservationMV.create_mv(engine, schema_tag=Role.VOCAB.value)

# Declaratively mapped: the mapped table's own schema is authoritative, no
# __mv_schema_tag__ needed (or consulted) at all.
class VocabPatientSummaryMV(Base, MaterializedViewMixin):
    __mv_name__ = "vocab_patient_summary"
    __mv_select__ = ...
    __tablename__ = "vocab_patient_summary"
    __table_args__ = {"schema": Role.VOCAB.value}
    patient_id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)

Every generated identifier is quoted through oa_configurator.qualified(), which quotes each component only when the dialect actually requires it (reserved words, mixed case, embedded quotes or spaces) — the same behavior every other Core-built query in this stack has.

docs.title: Failure handling and backend support
docs.text:
The built-in implementation is PostgreSQL-oriented. SQLite rejects materialized-view operations with NotImplementedError; this is intentional, not an emulation using ordinary views.

create_mv(), drop_mv(), and declared-index creation all wrap execution failures in MaterializationError.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
MaterializedViewMixin

Mixin providing materialized view lifecycle helpers.

Classes using this mixin must define:

  • __mv_name__: the name of the materialized view
  • __mv_select__: a SQLAlchemy Select defining the view contents
  • optionally, __mv_dependencies__: names of tables or materialized views this MV depends on
  • optionally, __mv_schema_tag__: the schema_translate_map key a Core-only declaration (no Base/mapped Table) resolves through. When the class is also declaratively mapped, its own mapped table's schema is used instead and __mv_schema_tag__ is ignored (see :meth:_resolve_schema_tag.)

This mixin does not define ORM mappings; it is intended for schema-level helpers used during migrations, setup, or administrative workflows.

Examples:

class RecentObservationMV(MaterializedViewMixin):

    __mv_name__ = "mv_recent_observation"

    __mv_select__ = (
        select(
            Observation.observation_id,
            Observation.person_id,
            Observation.observation_date,
            Observation.value_as_number,
            Concept.concept_id,
            Concept.concept_name,
            Concept.domain_id,
        )
        .join(
            Concept,
            Observation.observation_concept_id == Concept.concept_id
        )
        .where(
            Observation.observation_date
            >= func.current_date() - text("INTERVAL '30 days'")
        )
    )

__mv_select__ is a normal SQLAlchemy Select. No special syntax required.

By combining with declarative base, you can define columns to query the mv as an object too:

daily_counts_select = (
    select(
        Observation.observation_date.label("observation_date"),
        Observation.observation_concept_id.label("concept_id"),
        sa.func.count().label("n_observations"),
        sa.func.row_number().over().label('mv_id')
    )
    .group_by(
        Observation.observation_date,
        Observation.observation_concept_id,
    )
)

class DailyObservationCountsMV(Base, MaterializedViewMixin):

    __mv_name__ = "mv_daily_observation_counts"
    __mv_select__ = daily_counts_select
    __mv_pk__ = ["mv_id"]
    __table_args__ = {"extend_existing": True}
    __tablename__ = __mv_name__

    __mv_dependencies__ = {
        "observation",
        "concept",
    }

    mv_id = sa.Column(primary_key=True)
    observation_date = sa.Column(sa.Date, nullable=False)
    concept_id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, nullable=False)
    n_observations = sa.Column(sa.Integer, nullable=False)
Query like a normal mapped class:

rows = (
    session.query(DailyObservationCount)
    .filter(DailyObservationCount.observation_date >= date(2025, 1, 1))
    .order_by(DailyObservationCount.n_observations.desc())
    .all()
)

Best practices

  • No inserts / updates
  • Composite PK required for ORM identity map
  • Treat as immutable cache

resolve_mv_refresh_order

Resolve materialized view refresh order using topological sort.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If a dependency cycle is detected.

refresh_all_mvs

Handle refreshing multiple materialized views in dependency order.

Examples:

    ALL_MVS = [
        ObservationWithConceptMV,
        DailyObservationCountsMV,
    ]

    refresh_all_mvs(engine, ALL_MVS)

Bases: DDLElement

CreateMaterializedView

SQLAlchemy DDL element representing a CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW statement.

This custom DDL construct allows a SQLAlchemy Select construct to be compiled into a backend-specific CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW statement, enabling materialized view creation to be expressed using SQLAlchemy's DDL execution model.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Fully qualified, quoted name of the materialized view to be created (see oa_configurator.qualified). The compiler has no live bindable to qualify a bare name itself, so callers must qualify it first.

required selectable Select[Any]

A SQLAlchemy Select construct defining the query backing the materialized view.

required with_data bool

When False, emit WITH NO DATA.

True if_not_exists bool

When True, emit IF NOT EXISTS.

True

A simple column index declared on a materialized view.

Only plain column indexes are representable here (no expressions or partial predicates). That restriction is deliberate: it's what keeps "is this index eligible for CONCURRENTLY refresh" decidable from the declaration alone, without inspecting the live catalog first.

Create one declared index on a materialized view.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default target str

Fully qualified, quoted name of the materialized view to index (see oa_configurator.qualified).

required index MaterializedViewIndex

The index to create.

required if_not_exists bool

Emit IF NOT EXISTS so creating an already-present index is a no-op rather than an error.

True

Drop one materialized view.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Fully qualified, quoted name of the materialized view to drop (see oa_configurator.qualified).

required if_exists bool

Emit IF EXISTS so dropping an already-absent view is a no-op rather than an error.

True cascade bool

Emit CASCADE to also drop objects that depend on this view.

Base exception carrying structured materialization failure context.

Bases: MaterializationError

Raised when a concurrent materialized-view refresh is not eligible.

This can happen before execution when no eligible unique index is declared, or after execution when PostgreSQL rejects the refresh.

docs.text: Return the bind's backend, or raise when it has no materialized views.

docs.title: _resolve_schema_tag(schema_tag) classmethod
docs.text: Effective schema_tag for one lifecycle call. A declratively mapped class's own mapped table's schema is authoritative, overriding any __mv_schema_tag__.

docs.title: create_mv(bind, *, schema_tag=None, with_data=True, if_not_exists=True, create_indexes=True) classmethod
docs.text:
Create the materialized view if it does not already exist.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bind Connection | Engine

A SQLAlchemy Engine or Connection used to execute the DDL.

required schema_tag str | None

schema_translate_map key the view's own physical schema resolves through. See :meth:_resolve_schema_tag for the default when omitted: the mapped table's own schema if the class is declaratively mapped, else cls.__mv_schema_tag__.

None create_indexes bool

When True, create every index declared in __mv_indexes__.

True Notes

The underlying SQL is emitted via a custom DDL element and executed through the resolved backend. With the built-in backends, this means PostgreSQL. Unsupported backends raise NotImplementedError.

Examples:

with engine.begin() as conn:
    RecentObservationMV.create_mv(conn)

This emits SQL equivalent to:

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW IF NOT EXISTS mv_recent_observation AS
SELECT
    observation.observation_id,
    observation.person_id,
    observation.observation_date,
    observation.value_as_number
FROM observation
WHERE observation.observation_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

docs.title: refresh_mv(bind, *, schema_tag=None, concurrently=False) classmethod
docs.text:
Refresh the contents of the materialized view.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bind Connection | Engine

A SQLAlchemy Engine or Connection used to execute the refresh.

required schema_tag str | None

schema_translate_map key the view's own physical schema resolves through; see :meth:_resolve_schema_tag for the default.

Request concurrent refresh, requiring a declared unique index.

This method issues a backend-specific refresh statement. With the built-in backends, materialized views are PostgreSQL-only. Concurrent refresh semantics are not handled here.

Examples:

with engine.begin() as conn:

docs.title: ORMTableBase
docs.text:
ORMTableBase is the foundational mixin for all ORM tables in orm-loader.

It provides: - primary key introspection - column inspection - ID allocation helpers

It contains no domain logic.

This page is generated from in-code documentation.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Mixin for SQLAlchemy ORM-mapped tables providing structural introspection and helper utilities.

This base class intentionally avoids any domain or schema semantics and is designed to sit at the lowest level of a model hierarchy.

It provides: - mapper access - primary key discovery and extraction - column inspection helpers - required-field detection for ingestion - monotonic ID allocation support

docs.title: allocator(session) classmethod
docs.text:
Create an ID allocator initialised from the current table state.

The allocator is initialised using the current maximum primary key value and can be used to generate monotonically increasing identifiers in environments without database-managed sequences.

Used to support autoincrementing primary keys on dialects without native sequence support (e.g., SQLite).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default session Session

An active SQLAlchemy session.

required

Returns:

Type Description IdAllocator

An ID allocator initialised to the current maximum ID.

docs.title: column_defaults() classmethod
docs.text:
Return the default of each non-key column that has one that can be supplied.

A server default given as text and a scalar Python default are returned as the value itself. A server default given as a SQL expression is returned as that expression, for the database to evaluate. A callable or context-sensitive default cannot be supplied for a whole file, so its column is not listed. A primary key never takes a default, because a file has to name it.

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, Any]

A mapping of column name to the value, or SQL expression, of its default.

docs.title: mapper_for() classmethod
docs.text:
Return the SQLAlchemy mapper associated with this ORM class.

This is a thin wrapper around sqlalchemy.inspect that provides a single, explicit access point for mapper inspection.

Returns:

Type Description Mapper

The mapper associated with the ORM-mapped class.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If the class is not a mapped SQLAlchemy ORM class.

docs.title: max_id(session) classmethod
docs.text:
Return the maximum value of the primary key column.

This method only supports tables with a single-column primary key.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default session Session

A SQLAlchemy session.

required

Returns:

Type Description int

The maximum primary key value, or 0 if the table is empty.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the table has a composite primary key.

docs.title: model_columns() classmethod
docs.text:
Return the mapped columns a file can supply.

Columns are keyed by their database name, which is the name that file headers and staging tables use, even when Column.key differs. Computed columns are generated by the database and are not included.

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, ColumnElement]

A mapping of database column name to column object.

docs.title: pk_columns() classmethod
docs.text:
Return the primary key columns for the mapped table.

The columns are returned in mapper-defined order.

Returns:

Type Description list[ColumnElement]

A list of primary key column objects.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the table has no primary key defined.

docs.title: pk_names() classmethod
docs.text:
Return the primary key column names.

Returns:

Type Description list[str]

A list of primary key column names.

docs.title: required_columns() classmethod
docs.text:
Return column names that must be present in inbound data.

A column is required if it is a primary key, or if it is non-nullable and has no default that can be supplied (see column_defaults).

This method is intended for ingestion-time validation and does not attempt to enforce schema semantics beyond insert viability.

Returns:

Type Description set[str]

A set of required column names.

docs.title: sql_expression_defaults() classmethod
docs.text:
Return the defaults that are SQL expressions, which the database evaluates for each row.

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, ClauseElement]

A mapping of column name to its SQL expression default.

docs.title: SerialisableTableInterface
docs.text:
Mixin providing explicit, deterministic serialisation helpers for ORM row instances.

Supports: - dictionary conversion - JSON serialisation - stable row fingerprints

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Bases: ORMTableBase

Mixin for SQLAlchemy ORM tables providing explicit serialisation helpers.

This interface adds lightweight, deterministic helpers for converting ORM-mapped rows into dictionaries, JSON strings, and stable fingerprints.

It is intended for: - debugging and inspection - auditing and reproducibility checks - lightweight export or API layers - content-addressable comparisons

No assumptions are made about schema semantics or domain logic.

docs.title: __iter__()
docs.text:
Iterate over the ORM instance as (key, value) pairs.

This enables lightweight unpacking and interoperability with dictionary-based APIs.

Yields:

Type Description tuple[str, Any]

Column name and value pairs.

docs.title: __json__()
docs.text:
Return a JSON-serialisable representation of the ORM instance.

This hook is provided for compatibility with JSON encoders that check for a __json__ method.

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, Any]

A dictionary representation of the ORM row.

docs.title: fingerprint()
docs.text:
Compute a stable fingerprint for the ORM instance.

The fingerprint is derived from the JSON serialisation of the row with null values included and is suitable for: - change detection - deduplication - caching - reproducibility checks

Returns:

Type Description str

A SHA-256 hexadecimal digest representing the row content.

docs.title: to_dict(*, include_nulls=False, only=None, exclude=None)
docs.text:
Convert the ORM instance into a dictionary.

The output is derived directly from the mapped model columns and reflects the current in-memory state of the object.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default include_nulls bool

Whether to include keys whose values are None. Defaults to False.

False only set[str] | None

An optional set of column names to include. If provided, all other columns are ignored.

None exclude set[str] | None

An optional set of column names to exclude.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, Any]

A dictionary representation of the ORM row.

docs.text:
Serialise the ORM instance to a JSON string.

This method delegates to :meth:to_dict and applies a stable, deterministic JSON encoding with sorted keys.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default **kwargs Unpack[ToDictKwargs]

Keyword arguments forwarded to :meth:to_dict.

{}

A JSON representation of the ORM row.

docs.title: Typing Protocols
docs.text:
Structural protocols defining the expected interfaces for: - ORM table classes - file-loadable tables - serialisable row instances

Protocols allow infrastructure to remain decoupled from concrete base classes.

docs.title: ORMTableProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Structural protocol for ORM-mapped table classes.

This protocol defines the minimal structural surface expected of SQLAlchemy ORM table classes within orm-loader.

It is intentionally lightweight and model-agnostic, focusing on: - core SQLAlchemy table attributes - primary key introspection - column discovery helpers

This protocol is used for static typing, runtime checks, and to decouple higher-level infrastructure from concrete base classes.

docs.title: FileTableProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: ORMTableProtocol, Protocol

Structural protocol for ORM tables that load from files.

This protocol captures the expected interface for tables that can participate in staged, file-based loading workflows.

It defines the contract for: - staging table management - reader selection - file ingestion and merging semantics

No assumptions are made about the underlying database or schema.

docs.title: SerializedTableProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Structural protocol for ORM instances that support stable serialisation.

This protocol defines the expected interface for ORM row instances that can be converted to dictionaries, JSON strings, and deterministic fingerprints.

It is primarily used for typing and interoperability with downstream consumers such as validators, APIs, and audit tooling.
